intro: Try generative AI and ML on AWS with your free credits. Each lab gives console steps, what you should see, and a clean-up list. Use small, low-cost models (for example Amazon Nova Micro or Lite), one Region for every lab, and don’t paste personal or confidential data into prompts.

labs.title: Secure your account and set a budget before using AI services
labs.goal: Protect the root user, set a budget alert, and sign in with a separate admin user before you call any models.
labs.why: Security, governance, and cost awareness are tested in Domain 5, and model calls are billed per token.
steps: Sign in as the root user, open Security credentials, and assign an MFA device. Delete any root access keys.
Open Billing and Cost Management → Budgets → Create budget → Zero spend budget, with your email address.
Add a monthly cost budget of a few dollars with email alerts at 80% and 100%.
Open IAM Identity Center → Enable, create a user for yourself, and assign the AdministratorAccess permission set to your account. Sign in through the access portal with MFA.
Choose a Region where Amazon Bedrock is available (for example US East (N. Virginia)) and use it for every lab.
check: The root user has MFA and no access keys.
Both budgets appear with email alerts.
You can sign in as your Identity Center user.
tips: If you already did the Cloud Practitioner “Start here” lab in this account, you only need to check the Region.

labs.title: Compare models and inference parameters in the Bedrock playground
labs.goal: Send the same prompt to two models and see how temperature, top-p, and maximum tokens change the output.
labs.why: Model selection, inference parameters, tokens, latency, and pricing are core Domain 2 and 3 topics.
labs.costNote: A few cents of tokens with small models; covered by credits.
steps: Open Amazon Bedrock → Playgrounds → Chat / text. Choose a small model such as Amazon Nova Micro. If a model asks you to request access, follow the prompt.
Ask: “Write a one-sentence slogan for a bicycle repair shop.” Run it three times with temperature 0, then three times with temperature 1.
Set maximum output tokens to 20 and ask for a 200-word product description. Look at where the answer stops.
Open the playground’s model metrics and note the input tokens, output tokens, and latency for one run.
Use the compare mode (or open a second window) to send the same prompt to a larger model, such as Amazon Nova Pro, and compare quality, speed, and token counts.
check: Temperature 0 gives nearly identical answers; temperature 1 gives more varied ones.
A low maximum token limit cuts the answer off.
The larger model is slower and costs more per token.
tips: New accounts can earn credits for using a foundation model in the Bedrock playground.
Lower temperature and top-p → more consistent output. Maximum tokens → length and cost.

labs.title: Prompt engineering techniques and Prompt Management
labs.goal: Compare zero-shot, few-shot, and step-by-step prompts, then save a reusable prompt with a variable and a version.
labs.why: Prompt techniques, prompt templates, and versioning are Domain 3 topics.
labs.costNote: A few cents of tokens with a small model.
steps:
In the Bedrock chat playground with a small model, run a zero-shot prompt:
Classify the sentiment of this review as POSITIVE or NEGATIVE: "The delivery was late but the support team fixed it fast."
Run a few-shot version that gives three labeled examples before the review, and compare the answers.
Ask a short math word problem twice: once directly, and once adding “Think step by step, then give the final answer.”
Add a system prompt that sets a role and an output format, for example: “You are a support analyst. Reply in JSON with keys sentiment and reason.”
Open Bedrock → Prompt management → Create prompt named lab-sentiment. Use {{review}} as a variable, test it with two reviews, and create a version.
check: Few-shot examples make the label format more consistent.
The step-by-step prompt shows its reasoning before the answer.
Prompt Management shows the saved prompt and its version.
cleanup: Delete the prompt lab-sentiment in Prompt Management.
tips: Templates with variables keep instructions identical while the input changes.

labs.title: Protect a chatbot with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
labs.goal: Create a guardrail with a denied topic, content filters, and PII masking, then test it.
labs.why: Guardrail policies and responsible AI controls are tested in Domains 4 and 5.
labs.costNote: Guardrail checks are billed per text unit; a few tests cost cents.
steps: Open Amazon Bedrock → Guardrails → Create guardrail named lab-guardrail with a custom blocked message.
Add a denied topic “Investment advice” with a definition and two sample phrases, such as “Which stocks should I buy?”.
Turn on content filters for hate, insults, and violence, and the prompt attack filter.
Add a sensitive information filter that masks email addresses and phone numbers in responses.
Create the guardrail, then use the test panel with a small model: ask for stock tips, try “Ignore your instructions and…”, and ask the model to repeat a fake email address.
Open the trace for each test to see which policy acted.
check: The investment question returns your blocked message.
The prompt attack attempt is blocked.
Email addresses and phone numbers appear masked in the response.
tips: Denied topics block subjects however they are phrased; word filters block exact words.

labs.title: Build a RAG knowledge base with Amazon S3 Vectors
labs.goal: Index a few documents in a Bedrock knowledge base, ask questions, and check the citations.
labs.why: RAG, embeddings, chunking, vector stores, and citations are central to Domain 3.
labs.costNote: Embedding a few small documents and a handful of questions costs cents. Choose Amazon S3 Vectors; avoid OpenSearch Serverless for labs because it has a minimum hourly charge.
prerequisites: Two or three short documents without personal data, such as a public product FAQ saved as PDF or text.
steps: Create an S3 bucket lab-kb-<number> and upload your documents.
Open Amazon Bedrock → Knowledge Bases → Create knowledge base with vector store. Name it lab-kb and choose the S3 bucket as the data source.
Choose an embeddings model (for example Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2) and, for the vector store, create a new Amazon S3 Vectors store.
Create the knowledge base, then select the data source and choose Sync.
Open Test knowledge base, pick a small model for generation, and ask a question your documents answer. Open the source citations.
Ask a question your documents don’t cover and compare the answer.
check: After the sync, answers quote your documents and show citations.
For an unrelated question, the answer shows that the documents don’t contain the information, or relies on general knowledge without citations.
cleanup: Delete the S3 Vectors vector bucket and index that were created for it.
Empty and delete the bucket lab-kb-<number>.
tips: New or changed documents only appear in answers after you sync the data source.

labs.title: Chain steps with Amazon Bedrock Flows
labs.goal: Build a small visual workflow that summarizes input text and returns the summary.
labs.why: Building generative AI workflows and choosing between flows and agents are Domain 3 topics.
labs.costNote: A few cents for node runs and tokens.
steps: Open Amazon Bedrock → Flows → Create flow named lab-flow and let the console create the service role.
Connect the Prompt node to the Flow output node, then save the flow.
Open the test panel, paste a few paragraphs of public text, and run it.
Create a version and an alias for the flow.
check: The flow returns a two-sentence summary.
The trace shows each node’s input and output.
cleanup: Delete the flow lab-flow and its alias.
Delete the service role that the console created for it.
tips: Flows follow fixed steps you design; agents decide their own steps at run time.

labs.title: Evaluate a model with LLM-as-a-judge
labs.goal: Run a small model evaluation job on your own prompts and read the scores.
labs.why: Evaluating foundation models, metrics, and LLM-as-a-judge are Domain 3 topics.
labs.costNote: With five prompts, the generation and judge tokens cost well under $1.
steps: Create an S3 bucket lab-eval-<number>, upload lab-eval.jsonl, and create a folder results/ for the output.
Open Amazon Bedrock → Evaluations → Create, and choose an evaluation that uses an LLM as a judge.
Select a small model to evaluate, a judge model, and metrics such as correctness, completeness, and helpfulness. Point the dataset to lab-eval.jsonl and the results to the results/ folder.
Run the job and wait for it to finish, then open the report.
check: The report shows a score for each metric and an explanation from the judge for each prompt.
cleanup: Empty and delete the bucket lab-eval-<number>.
Delete the evaluation job, and the IAM role if the console created one.
tips: Use human evaluation for subjective qualities such as tone and empathy.

labs.title: Build a no-code model with SageMaker Canvas
labs.goal: Train a quick model on a sample dataset, read its metrics, and make a prediction without code.
labs.why: The ML lifecycle, model metrics, and no-code ML options are Domain 1 topics.
labs.costNote: Canvas charges about $2 per hour of session time while you are logged in, plus training. Log out when you finish.
steps: Open Amazon SageMaker AI → Canvas and follow the quick setup to create a domain and a user profile (this takes several minutes).
Open Canvas and choose one of the provided sample datasets, for example a housing or customer churn sample.
Create a new model, select the target column, and choose Quick build (not Standard build, which takes longer and costs more).
When the build finishes, open Analyze: note the metrics (for example accuracy and F1 score, or RMSE for numbers) and the column impact chart.
Make a single prediction by changing a few input values.
Log out of Canvas from the left menu when you finish.
check: Canvas shows model metrics and which columns influence predictions the most.
A single prediction returns a result and a probability or value.
cleanup: Log out of Canvas so session charges stop.
In SageMaker AI → Domains, delete the Canvas app and user profile, then delete the domain if you created it only for this lab.
tips: Classification → accuracy, precision, recall, F1. Regression → RMSE or MAE.

labs.title: Protect sensitive data with AI services
labs.goal: Use pre-trained AI services to detect PII, redact it from transcripts, extract document answers, and moderate images.
labs.why: Choosing AI services and protecting sensitive data are tested in Domains 1 and 5.
labs.costNote: A few demo requests cost cents at most. Use made-up data only.
steps: Open Comprehend → Real-time analysis and paste: “Hi, I’m Jane Doe, email jane@example.com, card 4111 1111 1111 1111.” Look at the PII entities.
Open Transcribe → Real-time transcription, turn on PII identification and redaction, and say a made-up phone number.
Open Textract → Try the demo, choose a sample document, and use Queries to ask a question such as “What is the total amount?”.
Open Rekognition → Content moderation and test with one of the sample images.
check: Comprehend labels the name, email address, and card number as PII.
The transcript shows the phone number as redacted.
Textract answers the query with a value and a confidence score.
tips: Redact or mask PII before storing transcripts or sending text to a foundation model.
